title: Physics
blurb: Energy, heat and waves in everyday life.

lessons.title: Energy & heat
lessons.summary: Where energy goes, how heat moves, and why heat pumps beat heaters.

cards.title: Energy changes form
cards.text:
Energy is never created or destroyed, only converted. A battery's chemical energy becomes electrical energy, which a bulb turns into light and heat.

Efficiency is the useful share. An old filament bulb turned about 5% into light; an LED manages several times that, so it runs cooler for the same brightness.

cards.title: Three ways heat moves
cards.text:
Conduction: heat passes through touching material, from the burner into the pan base.
Convection: warm fluid rises and cool fluid sinks, setting up loops that stir the water.
Radiation: infrared light travels across a gap with no material at all, like the warmth you feel beside a fire.

cards.title: Heat pumps move heat
cards.text:
A heat pump doesn't make heat; it moves it. A refrigerant absorbs heat from outside air (even cold air has some), the compressor squeezes it so it gets hotter, and it releases that heat indoors.

Because most of the heat comes from outside, 1 kWh of electricity can deliver 3–4 kWh of heat. That ratio is the COP.

cards.title: Specific heat
cards.text: The energy to heat something is mass × specific heat × temperature rise. Water's specific heat is high, about 4186 J per kg per °C, which is why it takes a while to boil and why it stores heat so well.

cards.title: Forms of energy
cards.text: Energy appears in many forms: kinetic (motion), potential (height, springs), thermal (heat), chemical (fuel, food), electrical, radiant (light) and nuclear. Physics tracks how it moves between them.

cards.title: Food energy
cards.text: Food energy is counted in kilocalories (kcal), shown on labels as "Calories". One kcal is about 4.2 kJ. A 2,000 kcal daily diet is about 2.3 kWh, roughly a 100 W bulb running all day.

cards.title: Thermal expansion in daily life
cards.text: Most things expand when heated: railway tracks have gaps, power lines sag in summer, a stuck jar lid loosens under hot water. Water is odd: it expands when it freezes, which is why ice floats and pipes burst.

cards.title: Insulation and the Thermos
cards.text: A vacuum flask stops all three kinds of heat transfer: the vacuum blocks conduction and convection, and silvered walls reflect radiation. That's why it keeps coffee hot or drinks cold for hours.

cards.title: Evaporation cools
cards.text: When water evaporates, the fastest molecules escape and take energy with them, so what remains cools down. Sweating, clay water jugs and cooling towers all use it.

cards.title: Where Earth's energy comes from
cards.text: Almost all energy we use traces back to the Sun: food, wind, hydro, solar and even fossil fuels (ancient sunlight stored by plants). The exceptions are nuclear, geothermal and tidal energy.

quiz.q: Which way does heat mainly reach you from the Sun?
quiz.explain: Space is nearly empty, so only radiation can cross it.

quiz.q: A heat pump with a COP of 3 uses 2 kWh of electricity. Heat delivered?
quiz.explain: Heat out = COP × electricity in = 3 × 2 = 6 kWh.

quiz.q: Heating 2 kg of water by 10 °C needs about…
Why does ice float?
options: Water expands when it freezes, so ice is less dense
quiz.explain: Ice is about 9% less dense than water.

quiz.q: How does sweating cool you?
options: Evaporation carries energy away from the skin
quiz.explain: The fastest molecules leave, taking heat.

lessons.title: Waves, sound & light
lessons.summary: One equation that covers guitar strings, Wi-Fi and thunderstorms.

cards.title: Anatomy of a wave
cards.text: A wave carries energy without carrying stuff along. Its wavelength (λ) is the distance from one crest to the next. Its amplitude is how tall it is, which sets loudness or brightness. Its frequency is how many crests pass each second, in hertz (Hz).

cards.title: Try it: how long is a sound?
cards.text: Speed equals frequency times wavelength. Sound travels at about 343 m/s in air, so low notes have long waves and high notes have short ones.

cards.title: How far away is the storm?
cards.text:
Light from lightning reaches you almost instantly; it travels about 300 000 km every second. Sound crawls along at about 343 m/s, roughly 1 km every 3 seconds.

Count the seconds between the flash and the thunder and divide by 3 to get the distance in kilometres.

cards.title: The electromagnetic spectrum
cards.text:
Radio, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet and X-rays are all the same thing: electromagnetic waves, all moving at the speed of light. Only the wavelength differs.

Shorter waves carry more energy per photon. That's why UV can burn skin and X-rays pass through it, while radio is harmless. Wi-Fi at 2.4 GHz has a wavelength of about 12.5 cm.

cards.title: Transverse and longitudinal
cards.text: In transverse waves, the medium moves at right angles to the wave (ripples, light). In longitudinal waves, it moves back and forth along the direction of travel (sound).

cards.title: Reflection and echoes

steps: Time it to find the distance

cards.text: Waves bounce off surfaces. An echo is reflected sound; sonar and ultrasound imaging time echoes to measure distance and see inside things.

cards.title: Interference
cards.text: When two waves meet, they add up: crests on crests make bigger waves, crests on troughs cancel. Noise-cancelling headphones play an inverted copy of outside noise to cancel it.

cards.title: Diffraction
cards.text: Waves bend around obstacles and spread through gaps comparable to their wavelength. That's why you can hear someone round a corner but not see them: sound waves are metres long, light waves less than a micrometre.

cards.title: Resonance

items: Wine glass broken by a voice
Bridges and machinery must avoid it

cards.text: Every object has natural frequencies. Push it at the right rhythm and the vibration grows, like pushing a swing. Musical instruments use resonance; engineers avoid it in bridges and machines.

cards.title: The Doppler effect
cards.text: A moving source squashes waves ahead of it and stretches them behind. An ambulance siren sounds higher as it approaches and lower as it leaves. Police radar and weather radar use the same effect.

quiz.q: A 343 Hz tone in air (343 m/s) has a wavelength of…
Thunder arrives 9 seconds after the flash. How far is the strike?
quiz.explain: Sound covers about 1 km every 3 s, so 9 s ≈ 3 km.

quiz.q: Which carries the most energy per photon?
quiz.explain: Shorter wavelength means higher frequency and more energy per photon.

quiz.q: Noise-cancelling headphones work by…
options: Playing sound that interferes destructively with the noise

quiz.q: Why does a siren sound higher as it approaches?
options: Its waves are squashed together (Doppler effect)

lessons.title: Describing motion
lessons.summary: Speed, velocity and acceleration.

cards.title: Speed
cards.text: Speed is distance divided by time. A car covering 120 km in 1.5 hours averages 80 km/h. To convert km/h to m/s, divide by 3.6.

cards.title: Speed vs velocity
cards.text: Velocity is speed with a direction. A car going round a roundabout at constant speed has a changing velocity, because its direction keeps changing.

cards.title: Acceleration
cards.text: Acceleration is how quickly velocity changes. A car going from 0 to 100 km/h (27.8 m/s) in 8 seconds accelerates at about 3.5 m/s².

cards.title: Free fall
cards.text: Near Earth's surface, falling objects speed up by about 9.81 m/s every second, if air resistance is negligible. After 1 s you're falling at about 35 km/h; after 3 s, over 100 km/h.

cards.title: Galileo's insight
cards.text: Without air resistance, heavy and light objects fall at the same rate. Astronauts on the Moon showed this in 1971 by dropping a hammer and a feather: they landed together.

cards.title: Terminal velocity
cards.text: As a falling object speeds up, air resistance grows until it equals the weight. Then it stops accelerating. A skydiver reaches about 200 km/h belly-down; a parachute cuts it to about 20 km/h.

cards.title: Stopping distance
cards.text: Stopping distance is thinking distance plus braking distance. Braking distance grows with the square of speed: double the speed, four times the braking distance.

cards.title: Reaction time

viz.unit: metres before braking starts (1 s reaction)

cards.text: A typical driver takes about 1 second to react. At 120 km/h, the car travels over 33 m before the brakes even start working. Phones at the wheel make it much longer.

cards.title: Relative motion
cards.text: Motion depends on the observer. On a train at 200 km/h, a coffee cup is still relative to you but moving fast relative to the ground. There's no absolute "stillness".

cards.title: Graphs of motion
cards.text: On a distance–time graph, slope is speed. On a velocity–time graph, slope is acceleration and the area underneath is distance travelled.

quiz.q: 90 km/h in m/s is…
If you double your speed, braking distance becomes about…
Without air, a hammer and a feather fall…

lessons.title: Newton's laws
lessons.summary: The three rules behind every push and pull.

cards.title: First law: inertia
cards.text: An object keeps doing what it's doing, staying still or moving in a straight line at constant speed, unless a net force acts on it. That's why passengers lurch forward when a bus brakes.

cards.title: Second law: F = m × a
cards.text: The acceleration of an object is proportional to the force on it and inversely proportional to its mass. Push twice as hard, it accelerates twice as fast; double the mass, half the acceleration.

cards.title: Third law: action and reaction
cards.text: Every force has an equal and opposite partner. When you push a wall, the wall pushes back on you. Rockets push gas backwards; the gas pushes the rocket forwards.

cards.title: Mass and weight again
cards.text: Mass (kg) is the amount of matter and doesn't change. Weight is the force of gravity on it and depends on where you are: on the Moon you'd weigh about a sixth as much.

cards.title: Seat belts and airbags
cards.text: In a crash, your body must lose its speed. Spreading that over a longer time and distance means a smaller force. Seat belts stretch a little and airbags cushion, cutting the peak force dramatically.

cards.title: Circular motion
cards.text: Moving in a circle needs a force towards the centre (centripetal force). On a roundabout it comes from tyre friction; for the Moon, from Earth's gravity. Without it, objects fly off in a straight line.

cards.title: "Centrifugal force"

items.r: your body keeps going straight while the car turns

cards.text: In a turning car you feel pushed outward. Really, your body is trying to go straight (inertia) while the car turns under you. The "centrifugal force" is how it feels from inside the turning frame.

cards.title: Friction and Newton

items: motion seems to need a push

cards.text: Things slow down on Earth because of friction and air resistance, not because motion naturally stops. In space, a nudged object keeps drifting for ever.

cards.title: Newton's laws in sport

items: Landing with bent knees reduces force

cards.text: Footballers push the ground backward to accelerate forward; heavier players are harder to stop; a well-timed kick transfers more force through a longer contact.

cards.title: Principia, 1687
cards.text: Isaac Newton published his laws of motion and universal gravitation in the "Principia Mathematica" in 1687. They explained falling apples and planetary orbits with the same rules.

quiz.q: A 1,000 kg car with a 2,000 N net force accelerates at…
Why do airbags reduce injuries?
options: They spread the stop over more time, reducing peak force
quiz.explain: Longer stopping time means smaller force.

quiz.q: Which law explains rocket propulsion?

lessons.title: Gravity and orbits
lessons.summary: Why the Moon doesn't fall down (it does, but misses).

cards.title: Universal gravitation
cards.text: Every mass attracts every other mass. The force grows with both masses and falls with the square of distance: double the distance, a quarter of the force.

cards.title: Orbits are falling
cards.text: An orbiting satellite is constantly falling towards Earth but moving sideways so fast that the ground curves away beneath it. Newton imagined a cannon on a mountain firing faster and faster.

cards.title: Orbital speeds
cards.text: The International Space Station orbits about 400 km up at about 28,000 km/h, circling Earth roughly every 90 minutes. Its crew sees about 16 sunrises a day.

cards.title: Weightlessness
cards.text: Astronauts in orbit aren't beyond gravity: at the ISS's height, gravity is about 90% as strong as on the ground. They float because they and the station are falling together.

cards.title: Geostationary orbit
cards.text: At about 35,786 km above the equator, a satellite takes exactly one day to orbit, so it stays above the same spot. TV and weather satellites use it.

cards.title: Tides

steps: Moon pulls the near side harder

cards.text: The Moon's gravity pulls more strongly on the near side of Earth than the far side, stretching the oceans into two bulges. As Earth rotates, most coasts get two high tides a day.

cards.title: Escape velocity
cards.text: To leave Earth without further thrust, you'd need about 11.2 km/s (40,300 km/h). Rockets don't reach it instantly; they burn for minutes, climbing and accelerating.

cards.title: Kepler's laws
cards.text: Planets move in ellipses with the Sun at one focus; they speed up when closer to the Sun; and the farther the planet, the longer its year, following a precise rule.

cards.title: Gravity assists

steps: Steal a little of its orbital energy

cards.text: Space probes swing past planets to gain speed, like a ball bouncing off a moving train. Voyager used Jupiter and Saturn to reach the outer Solar System.

cards.title: Gravitational waves

events.l: indirect evidence from a pulsar pair

cards.text: Einstein predicted that accelerating masses ripple space-time. In 2015 the LIGO detectors first measured these waves, from two black holes merging over a billion light-years away.

quiz.q: Why do astronauts float on the ISS?
options: They and the station are in continuous free fall together

quiz.q: Double the distance between two masses and their gravitational pull becomes…
What causes tides?
options: The Moon's (and Sun's) uneven pull across Earth

lessons.title: Momentum and collisions
lessons.summary: Why heavy, fast things are hard to stop.

cards.title: Momentum
cards.text: Momentum is mass times velocity. A slow lorry and a fast bullet can both have large momentum.

cards.title: Conservation of momentum
cards.text: In a collision with no outside forces, total momentum before equals total momentum after. It's how investigators reconstruct crashes.

cards.title: Elastic and inelastic
cards.text: In elastic collisions, objects bounce and kinetic energy is conserved (snooker balls, nearly). In inelastic ones, they deform or stick and energy turns into heat and sound (car crashes).

cards.title: Impulse
cards.text: Changing momentum takes a force applied over time: impulse. The same change can come from a big force over a short time or a small force over a long time.

cards.title: Crumple zones
cards.text: Car fronts are designed to crumple, extending the crash time from a few milliseconds to around a tenth of a second, which reduces the force on passengers.

cards.title: Recoil
cards.text: Firing a cannon pushes the cannon backwards: the shell's forward momentum is balanced by the cannon's backward momentum. The heavier cannon moves much more slowly.

cards.title: Newton's cradle
cards.text: Lift one ball, release it, and one ball flies out the other side. Momentum and energy pass through the stationary balls almost perfectly.

cards.title: Angular momentum
cards.text: Spinning objects have angular momentum. A skater pulling in her arms spins faster, because angular momentum is conserved while her shape becomes more compact.

cards.title: Gyroscopes
cards.text: Spinning wheels resist changes to their axis. Bicycles are stabilised partly this way; gyroscopes guide ships, aircraft and phones (as tiny vibrating sensors).

cards.title: Rockets in space
cards.text: Rockets need no air to push against: they push exhaust backwards and gain equal forward momentum. That's why they work even better in the vacuum of space.

quiz.q: A 0.5 kg ball at 10 m/s has momentum of…
Why do skaters spin faster when they pull their arms in?
options: Angular momentum is conserved as their shape becomes compact

quiz.q: What do crumple zones do?
options: Increase crash time to reduce forces

lessons.title: Gases and pressure
lessons.summary: Why tyres, balloons and weather behave as they do.

cards.title: Molecules in motion
cards.text: A gas is billions of molecules flying around at hundreds of metres per second, bouncing off each other and the walls. Their impacts on the walls are the pressure.

cards.title: Temperature and pressure
cards.text: Heat a closed gas and its molecules move faster, hitting the walls harder and more often, so pressure rises. That's why tyre pressures rise after a long drive.

cards.title: Boyle's law
cards.text: At constant temperature, squeezing a gas into half the volume doubles its pressure. Bicycle pumps and syringes show it.

cards.title: The ideal gas law
cards.text: Pressure, volume and temperature are linked in one equation for most gases at everyday conditions.

cards.title: Air pressure and altitude
cards.text: Air pressure halves roughly every 5.5 km of altitude. At the top of Serra da Estrela (1,993 m) it's about 80% of sea level; on Everest about a third.

cards.title: Boiling and altitude
cards.text: Water boils when its vapour pressure equals the air pressure. Up a mountain the air pressure is lower, so water boils below 100 °C and pasta takes longer to cook. Pressure cookers do the opposite.

cards.title: Balloons and density
cards.text: Hot air is less dense than cool air, so a hot-air balloon rises. Helium is lighter than air, so helium balloons float. A submarine changes its density with ballast tanks.

cards.title: Suction isn't pulling

steps: Air pushes on the drink's surface

cards.text: A drinking straw doesn't "pull" the drink up. You lower the pressure in your mouth, and the atmosphere pushes the liquid up the straw. That's why a straw can't lift water more than about 10 m.

cards.title: Compressed air
cards.text: Compressing air heats it (bike pump barrels get warm); letting it expand cools it (spray cans go cold). Fridges and heat pumps use this with special refrigerants.

cards.title: Weather and pressure
cards.text: High-pressure areas bring sinking air and usually settled weather; low-pressure areas bring rising air, clouds and rain. Barometers measure it, often in hectopascals (hPa).

quiz.q: Why does water boil below 100 °C on a mountain?
options: Lower air pressure means it boils at a lower temperature

quiz.q: Halve the volume of a gas at constant temperature and its pressure…
What pushes your drink up a straw?
options: Atmospheric pressure on the drink's surface
quiz.explain: You lower the pressure, the air pushes.

lessons.title: Light and optics
lessons.summary: Reflection, refraction, lenses and the eye.

cards.title: Light travels fast and straight
cards.text: Light travels at about 300,000 km/s in a vacuum and in straight lines (rays). It takes about 8 minutes 20 seconds to reach us from the Sun.

cards.title: Reflection
cards.text: Light bounces off a mirror at the same angle it hits it: angle of incidence equals angle of reflection. Rough surfaces scatter light in all directions, which is why paper isn't a mirror.

cards.title: Refraction

steps: Light enters water at an angle

cards.text: Light slows down in water or glass and bends as it enters at an angle. That's why a straw looks bent in a glass and pools look shallower than they are.

cards.title: Total internal reflection

steps: Hits the wall at a shallow angle

cards.text: Inside glass, light hitting the surface at a shallow enough angle is completely reflected. Optical fibres trap light this way, carrying internet data across oceans.

cards.title: Lenses
cards.text: Convex lenses bend light inwards to a focus: magnifying glasses, cameras, the eye. Concave lenses spread it out, used to correct short sight.

cards.title: The eye
cards.text: The cornea and lens focus light onto the retina, where rods (dim light, no colour) and cones (colour) turn it into nerve signals. The brain flips the upside-down image.

cards.title: Short and long sight
cards.text: Short-sighted (myopic) eyes focus distant objects in front of the retina; concave lenses fix it. Long-sighted eyes focus behind it; convex lenses fix it.

cards.title: Cameras
cards.text: A camera works like an eye: a lens focuses light onto a sensor of millions of pixels. Aperture controls how much light enters; shutter speed controls for how long.

cards.title: Rainbows
cards.text: Sunlight entering raindrops is refracted, reflected inside and refracted again on the way out. Each colour bends by a slightly different amount, spreading white light into a spectrum.

cards.title: Lasers
cards.text: A laser produces light of one colour, in step and in a narrow beam. Used in barcode scanners, fibre optics, surgery, cutting metal and measuring distance (lidar).

quiz.q: Why does a straw look bent in water?
options: Light refracts as it passes between water and air

quiz.q: What carries internet data across oceans using light?
options: Optical fibres, by total internal reflection
quiz.explain: Light stays trapped in the glass.

quiz.q: Short sight is corrected with…
quiz.explain: Concave lenses spread light so it focuses further back.

lessons.title: Colour
lessons.summary: Why the sky is blue and leaves are green.

cards.title: White light is a mix
cards.text: Newton showed with a prism that white light contains all colours. Each colour is light of a different wavelength, from red (about 700 nm) to violet (about 400 nm).

cards.title: Objects absorb and reflect
cards.text: A leaf looks green because chlorophyll absorbs red and blue light and reflects green. A black shirt absorbs most light (and gets hot in the sun); a white one reflects most.

cards.title: Mixing light vs mixing paint
cards.text: Light mixes additively: red + green + blue make white (screens). Paint mixes subtractively: each pigment absorbs some colours, so mixing many gives a muddy dark colour (printers use cyan, magenta, yellow, black).

cards.title: Why the sky is blue

steps: Blue comes from all over the sky

cards.text: Air molecules scatter short blue wavelengths much more than red ones (Rayleigh scattering). Scattered blue light reaches your eyes from all directions across the sky.

cards.title: Red sunsets
cards.text: At sunset, light crosses much more atmosphere. Most blue is scattered away before it reaches you, leaving reds and oranges.

cards.title: Seeing colour
cards.text: Your eye has three types of cone, most sensitive to roughly red, green and blue light. Every colour you see is your brain comparing their signals.

cards.title: Colour blindness
cards.text: About 8% of men and 0.5% of women of Northern European descent have some red–green colour vision deficiency, usually inherited. Good design never relies on colour alone.

cards.title: Infrared and ultraviolet
cards.text: Beyond red is infrared, which we feel as heat and which night cameras see. Beyond violet is ultraviolet, which causes sunburn and makes some materials glow.

cards.title: Colour temperature
cards.text: Light bulbs are described in kelvin: warm white about 2,700 K (yellowish), daylight about 5,000–6,500 K (bluish). Warm light feels cosier in the evening.

cards.title: Screens
cards.text: Every pixel on a screen has red, green and blue sub-pixels. Varying their brightness creates millions of colours. Zoom in on a screen with a magnifier and you can see them.

quiz.q: Why do leaves look green?
options: They reflect green and absorb red and blue

quiz.q: Why is the sky blue?
options: Air scatters blue light more than red

quiz.q: Mixing red, green and blue light gives…

lessons.title: Sound
lessons.summary: Loudness, pitch and how we hear.

cards.title: What sound is
cards.text: Sound is a pressure wave: a vibrating object pushes and pulls the air, creating compressions and rarefactions that travel to your ear.

cards.title: Pitch and frequency
cards.text: Pitch is how high or low a sound is, set by frequency. Humans hear roughly 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz; the upper limit falls with age.

cards.title: Loudness and decibels
cards.text: Loudness is measured in decibels, a logarithmic scale: every +10 dB is ten times the sound intensity and sounds roughly twice as loud.

cards.title: Hearing damage
cards.text: Long exposure above about 85 dB can permanently damage the tiny hair cells in your inner ear. Concerts and power tools call for earplugs.

cards.title: Speed of sound
cards.text: Sound travels about 343 m/s in air, roughly 1,500 m/s in water and around 5,000 m/s in steel. Sound needs a medium: in space, no one can hear you.

cards.title: Timbre
cards.text: A violin and a flute playing the same note sound different because each produces a different mix of overtones (harmonics) on top of the main frequency.

cards.title: Acoustics of rooms
cards.text: Hard surfaces reflect sound and make rooms echoey; soft furnishings, curtains and acoustic panels absorb it. Concert halls are designed for the right amount of reverberation.

cards.title: Ultrasound
cards.text: Frequencies above human hearing are used for medical imaging, cleaning baths, distance sensors and by bats and dolphins to navigate.

cards.title: Infrasound
cards.text: Very low frequencies below 20 Hz travel huge distances. Elephants communicate with them; volcanoes, earthquakes and nuclear tests are detected by infrasound monitoring stations.

cards.title: How we hear
cards.text: The eardrum vibrates, three tiny bones amplify the motion, and in the snail-shaped cochlea thousands of hair cells turn vibrations of different frequencies into nerve signals.

quiz.q: Every +10 dB means the sound intensity is…
Sound travels fastest in…
What makes a violin and flute sound different on the same note?

lessons.title: Atoms
lessons.summary: What everything is made of.

cards.title: Tiny and mostly empty
cards.text: An atom has a tiny, dense nucleus of protons and neutrons, surrounded by a cloud of electrons. If the nucleus were a marble in the centre of a football stadium, the electrons would be in the outer stands.

cards.title: Protons, neutrons, electrons
cards.text: Protons are positive, electrons negative, neutrons neutral. Protons and neutrons weigh about the same; an electron weighs about 1/1,836 as much.

cards.title: Elements
cards.text: The number of protons decides the element: 1 is hydrogen, 6 carbon, 8 oxygen, 26 iron, 79 gold. There are 118 known elements.

cards.title: Isotopes
cards.text: Atoms of the same element can have different numbers of neutrons: isotopes. Carbon-12 and carbon-14 are both carbon; carbon-14 is radioactive and used to date ancient remains.

cards.title: The periodic table
cards.text: Mendeleev arranged elements in 1869 by mass and properties, leaving gaps for elements not yet discovered, and predicted their properties. Columns group elements that behave alike.

cards.title: Electron shells
cards.text: Electrons sit in energy levels or shells. Chemistry is mostly about the outer electrons: atoms share, give or take them to form bonds and fill their outer shell.

cards.title: Molecules
cards.text: Atoms join into molecules: two hydrogens and an oxygen make water (H₂O); carbon and two oxygens make carbon dioxide (CO₂).

cards.title: States of matter
cards.text: Solids keep their shape, liquids take the container's shape, gases fill it. Heating gives particles more energy to break free. Plasma, a hot ionised gas, is a fourth state, found in stars and lightning.

cards.title: Seeing atoms
cards.text: Atoms are too small for light microscopes, but scanning tunnelling microscopes, invented in 1981, can image and even move individual atoms. IBM famously spelled its logo with 35 xenon atoms in 1989.

cards.title: Where atoms come from
cards.text: Hydrogen and helium formed in the Big Bang. Heavier elements were forged inside stars and in stellar explosions. The carbon in you and the iron in your blood were made in stars.

quiz.q: What decides which element an atom is?
Carbon-12 and carbon-14 are…
Where were most heavy elements, like the iron in your blood, made?

lessons.title: Radioactivity
lessons.summary: Unstable nuclei, radiation and half-lives.

cards.title: Unstable nuclei
cards.text: Some nuclei have an unstable mix of protons and neutrons. They release energy and particles to become more stable: that's radioactive decay.

cards.title: Three types of radiation

items: Beta: a few mm of aluminium

cards.text: Alpha particles (2 protons + 2 neutrons) are stopped by paper. Beta particles (electrons) by a few mm of aluminium. Gamma rays (energetic light) need thick lead or concrete.

cards.title: Half-life
cards.text: Each radioactive isotope has a half-life: the time for half of a sample to decay. After two half-lives a quarter remains; after ten, less than 0.1%.

cards.title: Half-lives vary hugely
cards.text: Some isotopes decay in seconds, others over billions of years.

cards.title: Carbon dating
cards.text: Living things take in carbon-14 constantly. When they die, it decays with a 5,730-year half-life. Measuring what's left dates organic remains up to about 50,000 years old.

cards.title: Background radiation
cards.text: We're always exposed to low natural radiation from rocks, soil, cosmic rays and our own bodies. Radon gas from granite rocks is the largest natural source, important in northern Portugal.

cards.title: Radon at home

items: Measure with a detector over 2–3 months

cards.text: Northern Portugal's granite releases radon, which can build up in basements and ground floors. Ventilation and sealing floors reduce it; inexpensive detectors measure it over months.

cards.title: Measuring dose
cards.text: Radiation dose to people is measured in sieverts (Sv), usually millisieverts (mSv). A chest X-ray is about 0.02 mSv; a CT scan several mSv; a flight Lisbon–New York about 0.04 mSv.

cards.title: Uses of radiation
cards.text: Radiation saves lives in medicine (X-rays, cancer therapy, sterilising equipment), checks welds in industry, powers spacecraft and detects smoke in alarms.

cards.title: Marie Curie
cards.text: Marie Curie discovered polonium and radium with Pierre Curie, coined the word "radioactivity" and won two Nobel Prizes, in physics (1903) and chemistry (1911), the first person to win in two sciences.

quiz.q: Which radiation is stopped by a sheet of paper?
quiz.explain: Alpha particles are large and heavy.

quiz.q: After 3 half-lives, how much of a sample remains?
What is the largest natural radiation source for many people?

lessons.title: Nuclear energy
lessons.summary: Fission, fusion and how reactors work.

cards.title: E = mc²
cards.text: Einstein showed that mass and energy are equivalent. A tiny amount of mass converts into an enormous amount of energy, because c², the speed of light squared, is huge.

cards.title: Fission
cards.text: A heavy nucleus like uranium-235 absorbs a neutron and splits into two smaller nuclei, releasing energy and two or three more neutrons, which can split more nuclei: a chain reaction.

cards.title: Inside a reactor
cards.text: Fuel rods heat water; the heat makes steam, which drives a turbine and generator, just like a coal plant but without combustion. Control rods absorb neutrons to keep the chain reaction steady.

cards.title: Energy density

items.l: per kg of natural uranium in a typical reactor

cards.text: One kilogram of uranium fuel can produce about as much energy as thousands of tonnes of coal. Nuclear power uses very little land and emits almost no CO₂ while operating.

cards.title: Nuclear waste
cards.text: Spent fuel is highly radioactive for thousands of years. It's small in volume and stored in cooling pools, then dry casks. Finland's Onkalo is the first deep geological repository being prepared for permanent disposal.

cards.title: Accidents
cards.text: The worst accidents were Chernobyl (1986), a flawed reactor design and unsafe test, and Fukushima (2011), where a tsunami knocked out cooling. They shaped strict safety rules worldwide.

cards.title: Portugal and nuclear
cards.text: Portugal has never had a nuclear power plant. A plan in the 1970s for one at Ferrel, near Peniche, was abandoned after local protests. It did mine uranium until 2001, at Urgeiriça and other sites.

cards.title: Fusion
cards.text: Fusion joins light nuclei, like hydrogen isotopes, into helium, releasing even more energy per kilo than fission. It powers the Sun. Doing it on Earth needs temperatures over 100 million °C.

cards.title: Fusion reactors
cards.text: Tokamaks like ITER, under construction in France, confine hot plasma with powerful magnets. In 2022 the US National Ignition Facility achieved a fusion reaction releasing more energy than its lasers delivered to the target.

cards.title: Small modular reactors
cards.text: SMRs are smaller reactors built in factories and shipped to sites, aiming to cut costs and construction times. Several designs are being developed and licensed worldwide.

quiz.q: What controls the chain reaction in a reactor?
Fusion joins…
Does Portugal have a nuclear power plant?
options: No, the Ferrel plan was abandoned

lessons.title: Relativity
lessons.summary: Einstein's ideas about space, time and gravity.

cards.title: Light speed is the same for everyone
cards.text: Einstein's 1905 starting point: the speed of light in a vacuum is the same for every observer, however fast they move. That simple rule forces space and time to stretch.

cards.title: Time dilation
cards.text: Moving clocks tick slower. At everyday speeds the effect is tiny, but at 87% of the speed of light, time passes at half the rate.

cards.title: The twin paradox
cards.text: If one twin flies to a distant star at near light speed and returns, she'll be younger than her twin who stayed on Earth. Experiments with fast particles and atomic clocks on planes confirm it.

cards.title: Nothing faster than light
cards.text: As an object speeds up, it takes more and more energy to accelerate it further. Reaching light speed would take infinite energy, so nothing with mass can do it.

cards.title: General relativity
cards.text: In 1915 Einstein described gravity not as a force but as curved space-time: mass bends space-time, and objects follow the curves. A heavy ball on a trampoline is the usual picture.

cards.title: Gravity slows time
cards.text: Clocks run slower in stronger gravity. A clock at sea level ticks slightly slower than one on a mountain. The effect is tiny but measurable.

cards.title: GPS needs relativity
cards.text: GPS satellite clocks run fast by about 38 microseconds a day overall (gravity speeds them up, orbital speed slows them down). Without correction, positions would drift by around 10 km a day.

cards.title: Bending light
cards.text: Gravity bends light. In 1919, during a solar eclipse, astronomers saw stars near the Sun shifted exactly as Einstein predicted, making him world-famous. Part of the observation was made on Príncipe island.

cards.title: Black holes
cards.text: If enough mass is squeezed into a small space, its gravity becomes so strong that not even light escapes. The boundary is the event horizon. The first image of a black hole was published in 2019.

cards.title: Energy and mass
cards.text: Special relativity also gave E = mc². In a nuclear reaction, the products weigh slightly less than the starting material; the missing mass became energy.

quiz.q: What stays the same for every observer in relativity?
options: The speed of light in a vacuum

quiz.q: Why must GPS correct for relativity?
options: Their clocks tick at a different rate, causing position errors
quiz.explain: Uncorrected, errors grow ~10 km per day.

quiz.q: According to general relativity, gravity is…
options: The curvature of space-time by mass

lessons.title: The quantum world
lessons.summary: How tiny things behave very strangely.

cards.title: Energy comes in packets
cards.text: At small scales, energy isn't continuous: it comes in packets called quanta. Light consists of photons, each with energy set by its frequency. Blue photons carry more energy than red ones.

cards.title: The photoelectric effect
cards.text: Shine light on a metal and it can knock out electrons, but only if each photon has enough energy. Dim blue light works; bright red light may not. Einstein explained this in 1905, earning his Nobel Prize.

cards.title: Wave–particle duality
cards.text: Light and electrons behave sometimes like particles and sometimes like waves. Fire electrons one at a time through two slits and they still build up a wave interference pattern.

cards.title: Uncertainty
cards.text: Heisenberg showed that you can't know both the exact position and the exact momentum of a particle at the same time. The more precisely you know one, the fuzzier the other becomes.

cards.title: Superposition
cards.text: A quantum system can be in a combination of states until measured. An electron's spin can be "up and down" at once; measuring it gives one definite answer, with probabilities set by the state.

cards.title: Entanglement
cards.text: Two particles can become linked so that measuring one instantly tells you about the other, however far apart. Einstein called it "spooky action at a distance". It can't send messages faster than light.

cards.title: Tunnelling
cards.text: Particles can sometimes pass through barriers they classically couldn't cross. Tunnelling powers the Sun's fusion, flash memory and scanning tunnelling microscopes.

cards.title: Quantum in your pocket
cards.text: Quantum physics isn't exotic: transistors, lasers, LEDs, solar cells, MRI scanners and atomic clocks in GPS all rely on it.

cards.title: Quantum computers
cards.text: Quantum computers use qubits that can be in superposition and entangled. For certain problems, like simulating molecules or breaking some encryption, they could vastly outperform normal computers, but building large reliable ones is very hard.

cards.title: Founders of quantum theory
cards.text: Planck (1900), Einstein (1905), Bohr (1913), Heisenberg and Schrödinger (1925–26) built quantum mechanics in about 25 years. It's the most precisely tested theory in science.

quiz.q: Why can dim blue light eject electrons when bright red light can't?
options: Each blue photon carries more energy

quiz.q: What happens when you measure a particle in superposition?
Which everyday technology relies on quantum physics?

lessons.title: The Solar System
lessons.summary: Our Sun, eight planets and much more.

cards.title: The Sun
cards.text: The Sun is an ordinary star, 109 times Earth's diameter, holding 99.8% of the Solar System's mass. It fuses about 600 million tonnes of hydrogen into helium every second.

cards.title: Eight planets
cards.text: Four small rocky planets (Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars) and four giants (Jupiter and Saturn of gas, Uranus and Neptune of ice). Pluto was reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006.

cards.title: Distances
cards.text: Distances are measured in astronomical units (AU): 1 AU is the Earth–Sun distance, about 150 million km. Neptune is about 30 AU away; light takes over 4 hours to get there.

cards.title: Venus: the hothouse
cards.text: Venus is closer in size to Earth but has a thick CO₂ atmosphere with a crushing 90 bar of pressure and surface temperatures around 465 °C, hotter than Mercury.

cards.title: Mars
cards.text: Mars is a cold desert with a thin CO₂ atmosphere, the largest volcano in the Solar System (Olympus Mons) and evidence of ancient rivers and lakes. Rovers like Perseverance search for signs of past life.

cards.title: Jupiter and Saturn

items.b: rings of ice, less dense than water

cards.text: Jupiter is so big that all the other planets would fit inside it. Its Great Red Spot is a storm larger than Earth. Saturn's rings are made of ice chunks and would float in a giant bathtub: its average density is less than water.

cards.title: Moons
cards.text: The Solar System has hundreds of known moons. Our Moon probably formed when a Mars-sized body hit the young Earth about 4.5 billion years ago.

cards.title: Asteroids and comets
cards.text: The asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter holds rocky leftovers. Comets are icy bodies from the outer Solar System that grow glowing tails when they near the Sun.

cards.title: Seasons on other planets
cards.text: Planets with tilted axes have seasons. Uranus is tipped on its side, so each pole gets about 42 years of continuous sunlight followed by 42 years of darkness.

cards.title: Age
cards.text: The Solar System formed about 4.6 billion years ago from a collapsing cloud of gas and dust. Meteorites give the most precise dates.

quiz.q: Which planet is the hottest?
quiz.explain: Its thick CO₂ atmosphere traps heat.

quiz.q: How far is 1 AU?
Why was Pluto reclassified in 2006?
options: It became classed as a dwarf planet
quiz.explain: It doesn't clear its orbit of other bodies.

lessons.title: Stars and galaxies
lessons.summary: How stars live and die, and how big the universe is.

cards.title: What a star is
cards.text: A star is a giant ball of hot gas held together by its own gravity, shining because nuclear fusion in its core converts hydrogen into helium.

cards.title: Light-years
cards.text: A light-year is the distance light travels in a year: about 9.5 trillion km. The nearest star after the Sun, Proxima Centauri, is 4.2 light-years away.

cards.title: Colours of stars
cards.text: A star's colour reveals its temperature: red stars are cooler (about 3,000 °C), our yellow Sun about 5,500 °C, blue stars over 20,000 °C.

cards.title: Life of a Sun-like star
cards.text: A star like the Sun burns hydrogen for about 10 billion years, swells into a red giant, sheds its outer layers and ends as a white dwarf. The Sun is about halfway through.

cards.title: Massive stars explode
cards.text: Stars many times the Sun's mass burn fast, then collapse and explode as supernovae, leaving neutron stars or black holes. The explosions spread heavy elements into space.

cards.title: Neutron stars
cards.text: A neutron star packs more than the Sun's mass into a ball about 20 km across. A teaspoon of it would weigh about a billion tonnes on Earth. Some spin hundreds of times a second as pulsars.

cards.title: The Milky Way
cards.text: Our galaxy is a barred spiral of perhaps 100–400 billion stars, about 100,000 light-years across. The Sun sits in an outer arm and takes about 230 million years to orbit the centre.

cards.title: Galaxies everywhere
cards.text: The observable universe holds hundreds of billions to around two trillion galaxies. The Andromeda galaxy, 2.5 million light-years away, is visible to the naked eye on dark nights and will merge with ours in about 4–5 billion years.

cards.title: Looking back in time
cards.text: Light takes time to travel, so we see distant objects as they were. We see the Sun as it was 8 minutes ago and Andromeda as it was 2.5 million years ago.

cards.title: Exoplanets

steps: Planet passes in front of its star

cards.text: Since the first confirmed in 1995 around a Sun-like star, over 5,000 planets have been found around other stars, mostly by tiny dips in starlight as they pass in front.

quiz.q: A light-year measures…
quiz.explain: How far light travels in a year.

quiz.q: What will the Sun eventually become?
quiz.explain: It's not massive enough to explode.

quiz.q: When we see Andromeda, we see it as it was…
quiz.explain: Its light took that long to arrive.

lessons.title: The universe
lessons.summary: The Big Bang, expansion and what we don't know.

cards.title: An expanding universe
cards.text: In 1929 Edwin Hubble found that distant galaxies are moving away from us, faster the farther they are. Space itself is expanding, like dots on an inflating balloon.

cards.title: The Big Bang
cards.text: Running the expansion backwards, the universe was once extremely hot and dense, about 13.8 billion years ago. The Big Bang wasn't an explosion in space but the expansion of space itself.

cards.title: The cosmic microwave background
cards.text: When the universe cooled enough for atoms to form, light could travel freely. That light, stretched into microwaves, still fills the sky at 2.7 K. Discovered by accident in 1965.

cards.title: Dark matter
cards.text: Galaxies spin too fast for the visible matter to hold them together. Something unseen adds extra gravity: dark matter. Nobody knows yet what it is.

cards.title: Dark energy
cards.text: In 1998 astronomers discovered the expansion is accelerating. Whatever drives it is called dark energy. It makes up most of the universe's energy content.

cards.title: How big is it?
cards.text: The observable universe is about 93 billion light-years across, larger than 13.8 billion × 2 because space expanded while light travelled. Beyond it, the universe may be infinite.

cards.title: Telescopes as time machines
cards.text: The James Webb Space Telescope, launched in 2021, sees infrared light from galaxies formed only a few hundred million years after the Big Bang.

cards.title: Elements from the early universe
cards.text: The Big Bang made mostly hydrogen and helium, with a trace of lithium. Everything heavier came later from stars, so the universe is still about 74% hydrogen and 24% helium by mass.

cards.title: Open questions
cards.text: Physicists still don't know what dark matter and dark energy are, why there's more matter than antimatter, or how to combine quantum mechanics with gravity.

cards.title: Our cosmic address
cards.text: Earth, Solar System, Orion Arm, Milky Way, Local Group, Virgo Supercluster, Laniakea Supercluster, observable universe.

quiz.q: How old is the universe?
quiz.explain: Measured from expansion and the cosmic background.

quiz.q: What is most of the universe's content?
Hubble discovered in 1929 that…
options: Distant galaxies are moving away, so space is expanding

lessons.title: The physics of weather
lessons.summary: Wind, clouds, rain and storms.

cards.title: The Sun drives the weather

steps: Warm air rises, cool air sinks

cards.text: The Sun heats the equator more than the poles and land more than sea. The atmosphere and oceans constantly move heat around to even it out, and that motion is weather.

cards.title: Wind
cards.text: Air flows from high pressure to low pressure. Earth's rotation deflects it (the Coriolis effect), so winds spiral around low-pressure systems: anticlockwise in the northern hemisphere.

cards.title: Clouds
cards.text: Rising air expands and cools. When it cools to its dew point, water vapour condenses on dust into droplets: a cloud. Each cloud type tells you something about the air.

cards.title: Rain

items: Ice crystals grow in cold clouds
Melt into rain as they fall
Or arrive as snow or hail

cards.text: Cloud droplets are tiny. Rain forms when droplets collide and merge, or when ice crystals grow in cold clouds and melt as they fall. A raindrop contains about a million cloud droplets.

cards.title: Humidity and dew

viz.unit: g of water per m³ of air (max, approx.)

cards.text: Warm air holds more water vapour than cold air. At night, air cools until it can't hold its vapour, which condenses as dew or fog. Relative humidity compares actual vapour with the maximum possible.

cards.title: Fronts
cards.text: Where warm and cold air masses meet, the warm air rises over the cold, forming clouds and rain. Atlantic fronts bring much of Portugal's winter rain, especially to the Minho.

cards.title: Thunderstorms
cards.text: Strong updrafts in warm, humid, unstable air build towering cumulonimbus clouds up to 12 km or more. Charge separates, producing lightning, thunder, heavy rain and sometimes hail.

cards.title: Sea breezes
cards.text: On sunny days, land heats faster than the sea. Air rises over the land and cooler sea air flows in: a sea breeze. At night it reverses into a land breeze. The Nortada on Portugal's coast is a summer wind linked to these pressure patterns.

cards.title: Forecasting
cards.text: Forecasts come from supercomputers solving the physics equations of the atmosphere on a 3D grid, starting from millions of observations. Accuracy for 5 days ahead today is roughly what 1-day forecasts were in the 1980s.

cards.title: IPMA warnings
cards.text: In Portugal, IPMA issues weather warnings in yellow, orange and red for rain, wind, heat, cold, sea agitation and more, by district.

quiz.q: Why does air rising form clouds?
options: It expands and cools to its dew point, so vapour condenses

quiz.q: In the northern hemisphere, winds circle low-pressure systems…
What causes a daytime sea breeze?
options: Land heating faster than the sea
quiz.explain: Warm air rises over land, sea air replaces it.

lessons.title: Great physicists
lessons.summary: The people who shaped how we understand the world.

cards.title: Archimedes (c. 287–212 BCE)
cards.text: The Greek mathematician from Syracuse discovered the principle of buoyancy and the law of the lever ("Give me a place to stand and I will move the Earth"), and estimated π.

cards.title: Galileo Galilei (1564–1642)
cards.text: Galileo used experiments and telescopes to study motion and the sky. He discovered Jupiter's four big moons and the phases of Venus, supporting the idea that Earth orbits the Sun.

cards.title: Isaac Newton (1643–1727)
cards.text: Newton gave us the laws of motion, universal gravitation, calculus (alongside Leibniz) and much of optics, showing that white light contains all colours.

cards.title: Michael Faraday (1791–1867)
cards.text: Faraday, largely self-taught, discovered electromagnetic induction, invented the first electric motor and dynamo, and introduced the idea of fields.

cards.title: James Clerk Maxwell (1831–1879)
cards.text: Maxwell united electricity, magnetism and light in four equations and predicted electromagnetic waves, opening the way to radio, TV and Wi-Fi.

cards.title: Marie Curie (1867–1934)
cards.text: Pioneer of radioactivity, discoverer of polonium and radium, the first woman to win a Nobel Prize and the only person to win in two different sciences.

cards.title: Albert Einstein (1879–1955)
cards.text: In 1905 alone he explained the photoelectric effect, Brownian motion and special relativity, including E = mc². In 1915 he published general relativity.

cards.title: Niels Bohr and Werner Heisenberg
cards.text: Bohr's 1913 model put electrons in fixed energy levels; Heisenberg's uncertainty principle (1927) and matrix mechanics helped build quantum theory. Their debates with Einstein shaped modern physics.

cards.title: Richard Feynman (1918–1988)
cards.text: Feynman helped develop quantum electrodynamics, famous for its precision, and was a celebrated teacher. He showed the cause of the Challenger shuttle disaster with a glass of ice water and an O-ring.

cards.title: Science is a team effort
cards.text: Famous names stand on the work of many others: experimenters, instrument makers, mathematicians and students. Today's discoveries, like the Higgs boson in 2012, involve thousands of scientists.

quiz.q: Who discovered electromagnetic induction?
Who united electricity, magnetism and light in four equations?
Who discovered Jupiter's four largest moons?
